subject: Banking
title: Why Savings Rates Are So Low
description: A 60-second lesson on Why Savings Rates Are So Low.

hook.text: Your savings account earns almost nothing. The bank lends your money at 7% and keeps most of the profit.

buildup.text: Banks set deposit rates based on competition. If most banks pay 0.5%, the market finds that acceptable.

discovery.text: Banks don't need to attract deposits aggressively. They have more deposits than loan demand in most periods.

twist.text: Online banks pay 4-5% because they have no branches. Your local bank spends that margin on real estate and tellers.

climax.text: Low savings rates aren't greed. They're the cost of branches, ATMs, and local presence passed on to depositors.

punchline.text: Your low rate funds the branch. Online banks skip branches and pay you more.

quiz.question: Why do online banks offer higher savings rates?
options: They have no branch costs to cover

details.summary: Banks deliberately pay low savings rates because the gap between what they earn on loans and pay on deposits is their primary profit source. Competition for deposits is limited because switching costs keep most customers from chasing better rates.
details.whyItMatters: Low savings rates effectively transfer wealth from savers to bank shareholders. When banks pay 0.5 percent on savings while earning 5 percent on loans, the 4.5 point spread is pure profit at the saver's expense.
takeaways: Large banks paid an average of 0.46% on savings while online banks offered 4-5% in 2023
Inertia and switching costs keep most deposits at low-paying institutions
Low savings rates are a deliberate strategy to maximize net interest margin

faq.question: Why do traditional banks pay so much less than online banks?
faq.answer: Traditional banks have branch networks and higher overhead that they fund through wider spreads. They also rely on customer inertia, knowing most depositors will not bother moving money for a better rate. Online banks with lower costs can afford to pay more.

faq.question: Should you move savings to a high-yield account?
faq.answer: On $10,000 in savings, the difference between 0.5% and 5% is $450 per year. High-yield savings accounts at FDIC-insured institutions offer the same safety with dramatically better returns. The biggest barrier is the effort of opening a new account.
